title: The City's Front Room
where: A1 Syntagma Sq., by the terminal; the Parliament is across Amalias
short: Welcome aboard. This is Syntagma, Constitution Square, and for Athenians it's the city's front room: the place you arrange to meet, cut across on the way to work, and come back to when something matters. The long, pale building across the avenue is the Parliament, which began life as the home of the young king and queen. In front of it, look for the guards in white pleated kilts. Every part of their uniform, down to the nailed red shoes, is still made by hand by the guard's own tailors.
long:
Welcome aboard, and settle in. This is Syntagma, which means Constitution. The square is named for a September night in eighteen forty-three, when Athenians and soldiers gathered under the palace windows and asked the king for a constitution, and got one. Ever since, this has been the city's front room. People arrange to meet here, cut across it on the way to work, sit by the fountain with a paper cup of iced coffee, and come back to it in their thousands whenever something matters, whether it's a celebration or a worry they want to share.
The long, pale building across the avenue is the Parliament. It was built in the eighteen thirties and forties as a home for King Otto and Queen Amalia, the first royal household of modern Greece, and behind it lies the garden the queen planted, which you'll pass a little later on the loop.
In front of the Parliament, look for the guards at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. They're the Evzones, young men doing their national service, and their uniform is a small museum of handcraft. The white kilt, the fustanella, takes around thirty metres of cloth and is said to have four hundred pleats. The red leather shoes, the tsarouchia, have a black pompom on the toe and weigh about three kilos each, with dozens of nails in the sole that ring on the marble as the guards march. All of it is still cut and sewn by hand, by a small team of tailors and embroiderers who work for the guard.
Every hour the guards change, with slow, swinging steps that look almost like a dance. Watch for the soldier who walks alongside them between moves and quietly straightens a tassel or a collar, much as a parent might tidy a child before the school photograph.
Under the square is the metro station, and when it was dug in the nineteen nineties, archaeologists found layers of the old city beneath it. Some of what they found is on show by the ticket barriers, behind glass, so Athenians pass a few thousand years of their own history on the way to work.
The full loop takes about an hour and a half if you stay aboard. Along the way, this track tells you less about battles and more about the people who lived here, then and now: who wove and who cooked, who sold coffee on the corner, and who planted the trees you'll be glad of in the afternoon.

title: Islanders Under the Rock
where: A2 Melina Merkouri / Plaka, at the edge of Plaka below the Acropolis (interchange with the Piraeus and Beach lines)
short: This neighbourhood is named for General Makrygiannis, a hero of the War of Independence who never went to school, and who taught himself to write as a grown man so he could set down his story in his own words. Up the slope is Plaka, the oldest lived-in part of Athens. Above it, tucked right under the Acropolis, are the little white houses of Anafiotika, built in the eighteen forties by stonemasons from the island of Anafi, who came to work on the king's new palace.
long:
This is Makrygianni, a neighbourhood of apartment blocks, bakeries and small hotels at the foot of the Acropolis, and it's named for a man whose story is a gentle one to begin with. Yannis Makrygiannis was a hero of the Greek War of Independence in the eighteen twenties. He grew up poor, never went to school, and couldn't read or write. Then, in his early thirties, he taught himself, slowly, letter by letter, because he wanted to write down what he had lived through in his own words. His memoirs, written in the plain spoken Greek of a villager, are now treasured as one of the great works of modern Greek prose.
Up the slope is Plaka, the oldest continuously lived-in part of the city. Its lanes are lined with nineteenth-century houses with tiled roofs and wooden shutters, courtyards full of pots of basil and geraniums, and old churches so small they'd fit inside a living room.
Above Plaka, right under the north face of the rock, is a pocket of whitewashed houses that looks as if someone had set a Cycladic village down in the middle of Athens. In a way, someone did. When Athens became the capital in the eighteen thirties, the new kingdom needed builders, and many came from the islands. A good number came from Anafi, a small island just east of Santorini that was known for its masons. They worked on the king's palace by day, and they needed somewhere to live.
The story goes that they made use of an old custom: if you could raise a house and put a roof on it between sunset and sunrise, it couldn't simply be pulled down in the morning. So they built by night, the way they built at home, in small white cubes with steps for streets, and they called the place Anafiotika, little Anafi. About forty-five of the houses remain, and some are still home to descendants of those first island families.
If you walk up there, go quietly. The lanes are so narrow you'll brush the walls, and the doors you pass are people's front doors. You'll soon meet the other residents: the cats, asleep on warm steps and in flowerpots. They're fed by neighbours and by volunteers who look after the cats of the whole Acropolis area, and they seem to know it.

title: The Maidens and the Empty Spaces
short: Under the museum, beneath glass, lies an ordinary Athenian neighbourhood of streets, houses, workshops and baths, lived in for well over a thousand years. Upstairs stand five of the six marble maidens, the Caryatids, who once carried a porch roof on the Acropolis on their heads. The sixth is in London. On the top floor, the Parthenon sculptures are laid out with pale copies for the pieces still in the British Museum, which the actress and minister Melina Mercouri spent years asking to bring home.
long:
As you pass the museum, look for the glass set into the ground in front of it. Through it, and under the building itself, you can see an Athenian neighbourhood that was found when the foundations were dug: streets, houses, workshops and bathhouses, lived in from the age of the Parthenon into Byzantine times. There are wells and drains and kitchen floors, the ordinary bones of daily life. The museum was raised on pillars so the neighbourhood could stay where it was, and visitors can now walk down among the houses themselves.
On the first floor stand five young women in marble. They're the Caryatids, although the ancient building accounts simply call them the korai, the maidens. They once held up the roof of a small porch on the Acropolis, carrying it on their heads as calmly as if it were a basket. If you go in, look at their hair. Each has her own arrangement of braids, with a thick plait down the back that also strengthens the neck, where the stone is weakest. Each once held a shallow bowl for offerings.
They were brought indoors in nineteen seventy-nine to protect them from the city's air, and between twenty eleven and twenty fifteen conservators cleaned them very gently with a specially built laser, while visitors watched. There were six. The sixth was taken to Britain in the early eighteen hundreds and stands in the British Museum.
On the top floor, the glass gallery is turned to line up with the Parthenon, which you can see through its windows. Around the walls runs the frieze, the long band of carving that shows the procession to honour Athena. Where the original pieces are in London, there are pale plaster copies, so the gaps are plain to see.
Those gaps were the cause of Melina Mercouri's life. She was a film star first, famous around the world after Never on Sunday in nineteen sixty, then a campaigner against the military dictatorship, and from nineteen eighty-one Greece's first woman Minister of Culture. In July nineteen eighty-two, at a UNESCO conference in Mexico City, she asked formally for the marbles to come home, and the delegates gave her a long ovation. She argued for years for a new museum, a home ready to receive them. She died in nineteen ninety-four and never saw this building, which opened in twenty oh nine. Many Athenians still think of the empty spaces upstairs as hers.

title: A Robe for Athena
where: A4 The Acropolis & Parthenon, the walk up from the west end of Dionysiou Areopagitou, by Philopappou Hill (interchange)
short: Up on the rock, beside the Parthenon, Athena's oldest statue was carved from olive wood, and at her great festival the city brought her a gift that women made: a new woven robe. Young girls, chosen to live on the Acropolis for a year, helped set up the loom, and women of the city wove it. Down here, the stone paths up the hills were laid by hand in the nineteen fifties. And on Clean Monday each spring, Philopappou Hill fills with families flying kites.
long:
This is where many people step off for the walk up to the Acropolis. Up on the rock, the Parthenon is the building everyone photographs, but the one that mattered most to everyday worship was the smaller temple beside it, the Erechtheion, with the porch of the maidens. Inside it stood Athena's oldest and holiest image, a statue carved from olive wood. An olive tree grows beside it today, planted in modern times where Athena's own tree was said to stand.
At Athena's great summer festival, the Panathenaia, the city brought that old statue a gift: a new robe, a peplos, woven from wool. And the making of it was women's work from start to finish. About nine months before the festival, at another feast, two young girls called the arrephoroi, somewhere between seven and eleven years old, helped the priestess set up the threads on the loom. These girls were chosen from Athenian families to live up on the Acropolis for a year, and we're told they even had a special place up there to play ball. The weaving itself was taken on by women of the city, called the ergastinai, the workers, both young girls and older women.
When the robe was finished, it was carried through the city in a great procession and up the rock. In the museum, at the very centre of the carved frieze, there's a quiet scene of a cloth being folded, which many people take to be that same robe.
The paths you'll walk on here were made with the same kind of patient handwork. Between nineteen fifty-four and nineteen fifty-seven, the architect Dimitris Pikionis worked with his students and local stonemasons, with hardly any drawings, to lay the paths up towards the Acropolis and across Philopappou Hill. They used stones and pieces of marble saved from old Athenian houses that were being pulled down, and fitted them into the hillside like a patchwork quilt. It's worth looking down as you walk.
Philopappou Hill is also where Athenians come to play. On Clean Monday, the first day of Lent, families climb up with picnics and homemade kites, and the sky over the hill fills with them. On summer evenings, people come up simply for the light, to watch the marble turn gold and then rose as the sun goes down. On the next low hill, the Pnyx, the men of the ancient assembly once met to vote. Their wives and daughters weren't among them, but the city those men argued over was fed and clothed, and its goddess dressed, by the women at home.

title: A Basket on a Rope
where: A5 Temple of Zeus, by Hadrian's Arch on Amalias Avenue
short: The tall columns ahead belong to the Temple of Olympian Zeus, which took about six hundred and forty years to finish. Long after its gods had gone, people went on living around it, and for a while, on top of it. Until the eighteen hundreds, hermits lived in a little hut on the stone beam across two of the columns, and Athenians brought them bread and fruit, which they pulled up in a basket on a rope. Opposite the arch, look for a marble bust in a small garden: that's Melina Mercouri.
long:
Look for the tall columns standing in a wide field of grass and stone. This is the Temple of Olympian Zeus. It was begun by the city's rulers in the sixth century before Christ and finished by the Roman emperor Hadrian about six hundred and forty years later, which may make any unfinished projects at home feel a little less overdue. Of more than a hundred columns, fifteen still stand, and one more lies on the ground, just as a storm blew it down in eighteen fifty-two.
For centuries after it stopped being a temple, people simply lived around it, and for a time someone lived on top of it. Hermits called stylites, who chose to live on top of pillars to be nearer to God, set up a small hut on the stone beam across two of the columns, high above the ground. Athenians still remembered the last of them in the eighteen hundreds. One old Athenian recalled being taken there as a child to bring the hermit gifts of bread and fruit, which he gathered in by letting down a basket on a rope. The hut was finally taken down in eighteen seventy.
Just beyond the temple, the little Ilissos river once ran, though it's mostly hidden under the streets now. A spring on its bank, called Kallirrhoe, the beautiful stream, gave the water that Athenian brides were bathed in before their weddings, a custom the historian Thucydides still knew. It's easy to imagine women coming down here with water jars on the morning of a wedding, talking over the plans.
The arch by the road was put up in Hadrian's time, where the old town met the new quarter. On one side, its inscription says, this is Athens, the ancient city of Theseus, and on the other, this is the city of Hadrian, and not of Theseus. It's not so different from a sign on the edge of a town, telling you which neighbourhood you're in.
Opposite the arch, by the roadside, look for a marble bust in a small garden. That's Melina Mercouri, whom you met at the museum, unveiled here in nineteen ninety-nine, a few years after her death. She sits beside one of the busiest roads in the city, with the Acropolis she campaigned for not far behind her.

title: The Queen's Garden
where: A6 Parliament / National Gardens on Amalias Avenue (served twice: A6a now, A6b after the stadium)
short: Behind the railings is the National Garden, which began as Queen Amalia's own garden behind the palace in eighteen thirty-eight. She brought hundreds of kinds of plants to a dry, dusty town, and is said to have spent hours here every day. Today it belongs to everyone: grandparents with prams, office workers on benches at lunchtime, ducks and turtles on the pond, and plenty of cats. In summer it's noticeably cooler than the avenue, so if you hop off, it's a good place to catch your breath.
long:
Behind the railings and the tall trees is the National Garden, and it began with one young woman. Amalia of Oldenburg was still a teenager when she married King Otto, and she arrived in Athens in eighteen thirty-seven to find a small, dusty town with hardly a tree to sit under. From eighteen thirty-eight she set about making a garden behind the palace. A German gardener, Friedrich Schmidt, brought in more than five hundred kinds of plants, along with peacocks, ducks and turtles. The queen is said to have spent hours there every day, and she had a favourite rock where she liked to sit.
Amalia loved to ride and to dance, and Athenians grew used to seeing her on horseback around the town. She also put together a court dress drawn from Greek folk costume, with an embroidered jacket, a long silk skirt and a little cap, and it caught on so well that the Amalia, as it's still called, became one of the national costumes of Greek women, worn today at festivals and parades. In eighteen sixty-two the king and queen were made to leave Greece, and she never came back. Her garden stayed.
In the twentieth century it was opened to everyone and renamed the National Garden, and now it's the city's shared back garden. Grandparents push prams along the shady paths, office workers eat lunch on the benches, and children feed the ducks on the pond and hunt for turtles sunning themselves on the stones. Cats doze under the hedges, keeping a polite eye on the ducks. On a hot afternoon it's noticeably cooler under the trees than out on the avenue.
At the far side of the garden is the Zappeion, a grand hall with a curved colonnade, opened in eighteen eighty-eight. During the first modern Olympics, in eighteen ninety-six, it was the fencing hall, and in twenty oh four it was the press centre. In May nineteen seventy-nine, Greece signed its way into the European Community in its marble courtyard.
Nearby, among the trees, is Aigli, one of the oldest open-air cinemas in the city. On a summer night, a deckchair, the smell of jasmine and a film under the stars are a very Athenian way to end a hot day, and it all happens in a garden that a young queen planted nearly two centuries ago.

title: Embroidery and Coffee
where: A7 The 4 Museums, on Vasilissis Sofias: Benaki, Cycladic, Byzantine & Christian, War Museum
short: This stretch of avenue is lined with museums, and one of them was once a family's home. The Benaki Museum opened in nineteen thirty-one in the Benakis family mansion, and its folk costumes and embroidery show the patient handwork of generations of Greek women. Up the slope is Kolonaki, where Athenians can happily make a single iced coffee last all afternoon. Above it rises Lycabettus, the highest hill in the city, with a little white chapel on its summit.
long:
This stretch of Vasilissis Sofias is sometimes called the museum mile, and some of its museums began very close to home. The Benaki Museum, on the corner of Koumbari Street, was the house of the Benakis family. Antonis Benakis, a collector who grew up in Alexandria in Egypt, gave the house and his collections to the nation, and it opened as a museum in April nineteen thirty-one.
His younger sister, Penelope Delta, became one of the best-loved children's writers in Greece. In nineteen thirty-two she published a book about him called Trelantonis, Crazy Antonis, full of his childhood mischief in Alexandria, climbing, breaking things and leading his brothers and sisters into trouble. Generations of Greek children have grown up with it, so for many visitors the serious collector who founded the museum is also the naughty boy from a favourite book.
Inside, the rooms of folk costume and embroidery are among the most moving in the city. Before machines, almost every girl in a Greek village learned to spin, weave and embroider, and for years she worked on the linens, cushions and clothes for her dowry. Each region had its own patterns and colours, so a woman's dress told you where she came from, whether she was married, and how skilled her hands were. These were clothes for working and clothes for weddings, mended carefully and handed down.
Close by, the Museum of Cycladic Art grew out of the collection of Nicholas and Dolly Goulandris, and opened in nineteen eighty-six. Its small marble figures from the Aegean islands are between four and five thousand years old. Most are women, standing with their arms folded across their bodies, so simple and calm they look almost modern. Nobody knows quite what they meant to the people who made them.
Up the slope is Kolonaki, a neighbourhood of small shops, galleries and cafés, where Athenians are quite happy to make one freddo espresso last all afternoon while they watch the street go by. Nobody will hurry you. Above it all rises Lycabettus, the highest hill in the city, with the little white chapel of Saint George on top. A small funicular railway runs up inside the hill, and at sunset the whole city spreads out beneath you, white and gold, all the way to the sea.

title: Pictures of Home
where: A8 National Gallery / Hilton & Caravel Hotels, by Rizari Park
short: The big white hotel here opened in nineteen sixty-three as the Athens Hilton, and on its broad end walls the painter Yiannis Moralis carved huge figures into the marble: Athena, an olive tree and an owl, musicians with pipes, and women carrying baskets of offerings on their heads. Across the avenue is the National Gallery, which reopened in twenty twenty-one after eight years of work. Many of its best-loved paintings are scenes of ordinary Greek life, from children at play to the light on the countryside.
long:
The long white hotel here opened in nineteen sixty-three as the Athens Hilton, the first big international hotel of its kind in the city. Plenty of Athenians disliked it at first, a modern block rising so close to the classical skyline, but it soon became part of the city's life, the place for a special night out, and recently it has reopened under a new name.
Look at its broad end walls. The painter Yiannis Moralis designed a pair of enormous reliefs for them, carved line by line into about five hundred and twenty marble slabs. In them you can find Athena, the sun, an olive tree and an owl, a ship, musicians playing pipes, and young women carrying baskets on their heads, the offering-bearers of the ancient processions, here to welcome travellers instead of gods.
Across the avenue is the National Gallery, which also carries the name of Alexandros Soutsos, the collector who left his paintings and his fortune to the nation. It reopened in March twenty twenty-one, for the two hundredth anniversary of Greek independence, after eight years of rebuilding. The painter Georgios Iakovidis, who was the gallery's first curator, is loved for his pictures of children and family life, above all one called Children's Concert, painted around nineteen hundred, in which a group of small children make music on toy instruments with enormous seriousness. Many of the Greek painters of the eighteen hundreds turned in the same way to everyday life: village customs, harbours, portraits of their neighbours, and the clear, strong light that anyone who has spent a day in Athens will recognise.
Beside the gallery, Rizari Park is a small green square where people walk their dogs, sit with a book, or wait for a bus in the shade. A little further along is the Megaron, the city's great concert hall, where Athenians dress up for an evening of music and spill out afterwards into the warm night to talk it over at a café.
If you have time to step inside the gallery, it's a good antidote to the marble: a chance to see how Greeks have painted themselves, their homes and their children, in the years since the country became independent.

title: The Water Carrier and the Woman Who Ran
where: A9 Ancient Olympic Stadium, the Panathenaic or Kallimarmaro
short: Athenians call this the Kallimarmaro, the beautiful marble. It hosted the first modern Olympics in eighteen ninety-six, and the marathon was won by Spyridon Louis, a water carrier from the village of Marousi, who asked the king for nothing more than a cart and a donkey for his work. The day after, a woman named Stamata Revithi ran the same course on her own, and had to finish outside, because she wasn't allowed in. Today Athenians jog around it in the early morning.
long:
The horseshoe of white marble is the Panathenaic Stadium, which Athenians call the Kallimarmaro, the beautiful marble. There was a stadium here in ancient times for the games of Athena's festival, and in the eighteen nineties it was rebuilt in gleaming marble for the first modern Olympic Games, held here in the spring of eighteen ninety-six.
The race everyone remembers is the marathon, run from the town of Marathon to this stadium. It was won by a young man named Spyridon Louis, from the village of Marousi north of the city. He was a water carrier. His father sold water in Athens, and Spyridon helped bring it in. The story goes that he even stopped along the way for a glass of wine. When he came into the stadium first, the crowd went wild. Afterwards the king asked what he would like as a reward, and Louis asked for a small cart and a donkey, to make the water round easier. He never raced again, and went home to a quiet life in Marousi. The main Olympic stadium of twenty oh four, which stands there today, carries his name.
Women weren't allowed to compete in eighteen ninety-six at all. But the day after the men's race, a woman named Stamata Revithi set off alone from Marathon and ran the whole course, in about five and a half hours. She had people sign their names to say when she started and finished, so that no one could doubt her. When she reached the stadium she wasn't allowed in, so she finished outside. We know very little about the rest of her life. Today women run this course in their thousands.
The stadium is still part of the city's routine. Early in the morning, before the visitors arrive, you can buy a ticket to jog around the track, and many Athenians walk or run on the paths around the outside at dawn and dusk. Every November, the Athens Marathon follows the old route and finishes here, and runners of every age come in, tired and beaming, to the cheers of families up in the marble seats.
And each time the Olympic Games come round, the flame that's been lit at ancient Olympia is handed over on this track to the next host city, so for a moment the whole world's eyes turn to a stadium where a water carrier once won the day.

title: The Right to Read
where: A10 National Library, on Panepistimiou beside the University and the Academy
short: Along this avenue stand three white neoclassical buildings, the Academy, the University and the old National Library, built in the eighteen hundreds as the young Greek state's statement of faith in learning. For decades, though, those doors opened mainly to men. In eighteen ninety the University accepted its first woman student, Ioanna Stefanopoli, and in eighteen ninety-three two sisters, Angeliki and Alexandra Panagiotatou, began to study medicine here.
long:
This avenue is officially called Eleftheriou Venizelou, but everyone knows it as Panepistimiou, University Street. Look for three white buildings side by side, often called the Trilogy. The University in the middle was designed by the Danish architect Christian Hansen and begun in eighteen thirty-nine, and the Academy and the National Library on either side were designed by his younger brother, Theophil. For a new country where many people couldn't read, these were buildings of hope, a promise that the children of farmers and sailors could come and study here. If you can, look up at the University's porch, where there's a long painted frieze in soft colours.
For most of the eighteen hundreds that promise was made to boys. Girls might go to school, but few people expected them to go further. Then, in eighteen eighty-seven, a teacher and writer named Kallirroi Parren started a weekly paper called the Ladies' Newspaper, written and run by women. Its first issue sold out. Week after week it argued, patiently and persistently, that women should be able to study at every level and to earn their own living.
In eighteen ninety, the University accepted its first woman student, Ioanna Stefanopoli, at the School of Philosophy. In eighteen ninety-three, two sisters, Angeliki and Alexandra Panagiotatou, were admitted to the medical school, and in eighteen ninety-seven Angeliki became the first woman to graduate from it. Not everyone welcomed them, and it took real courage simply to walk up those steps each morning. Angeliki went on to a long career as a doctor and a teacher of medicine.
Today the steps are full of students again, waiting for friends, arguing, and sharing a koulouri, the ring of bread crusted with sesame that's sold from carts on almost every corner of the city. The National Library has moved its books to a new home by the sea, but the old building with its grand staircase still stands as Theophil Hansen designed it.
So as you pass, you might picture a young woman in the eighteen nineties, books held tight, climbing those marble steps for the first time while the whole street watched, and making it a little easier for everyone who came after her.

title: Small Lives, Long Ago
where: A11 National Archaeological Museum, on 28 Oktovriou (Patission)
short: This is the National Archaeological Museum, one of the great museums of the world. Among the gold and the famous bronzes, look for the small, human things: a little boy riding a galloping horse, a gravestone where a woman picks a necklace from her jewellery box, and bright wall paintings from the buried town of Akrotiri on Santorini, with swallows over red lilies and two small boys boxing. Next door is the Polytechnic, where every November people lay red flowers at the old iron gate.
long:
The long neoclassical building behind its gardens is the National Archaeological Museum, which holds treasures from all over Greece. It's easy to be dazzled by the gold, but walk a little further and you start to meet people.
Upstairs is a room of wall paintings from Akrotiri on Santorini, the town that was buried by an eruption about thirty-six hundred years ago. They were painted on the walls of people's houses. In one room, red lilies grow out of rocky hills while swallows swoop between them, some meeting in mid-air. In another, two small boys, each with a single boxing glove, spar with tremendous seriousness. Whoever lived in those rooms woke up every morning to spring flowers and children at play.
Downstairs are the carved gravestones of Classical Athens, and they're tender rather than sad. One of the loveliest belongs to a woman named Hegeso, from about four hundred years before Christ, and it was found in the old cemetery at Kerameikos. She sits on a chair with her feet on a footstool, while a young servant girl holds out an open jewellery box. Hegeso has lifted out a piece of jewellery and is looking at it, as she must have done on a thousand ordinary mornings. Her family chose to remember her like that, at home and unhurried.
In the great bronze hall, look for a small boy, perhaps ten years old, riding a galloping horse, leaning forward with his face set in concentration. He was found in pieces in the sea off Cape Artemision, and has been patiently put back together. He may be the most alive thing in the building.
Next door is the old Polytechnic, the university for engineers. In November nineteen seventy-three, under the military dictatorship, students occupied it and broadcast calls for freedom from a small radio station, until the gate was forced open in the early hours of the seventeenth. Lives were lost in those days. Every year around that date, Athenians come in their thousands to lay red flowers on the old iron gate, and schools mark the day. It's a quiet, steady kind of remembering, and the gate is kept just as it was.

title: Kiosks and Newcomers
short: Omonia means concord, and this busy square is where a great many newcomers have first met the city: villagers arriving to look for work, and, after nineteen twenty-two, refugees from Asia Minor who changed Athens for good. On the corners, look for the kiosks, the periptera. The first licences to run them were given to men wounded in the wars, in place of a pension, and they still sell almost everything, from newspapers and bus tickets to ice cream, cold water and phone chargers.
long:
Omonia means concord, or harmony, which is a hopeful name for one of the busiest squares in Athens. It's a crossroads of avenues, metro lines and buses, and for well over a century it's been where newcomers first met the city. People from villages all over Greece stepped off here looking for work. Later came people from Albania and Africa, Pakistan and Bangladesh and the Middle East, and the streets around still hum with their shops, their food and their languages.
The largest arrival of all came after nineteen twenty-two. When the war in Asia Minor ended in defeat, Greeks whose families had lived for generations along the Turkish coast and inland, in cities like Smyrna, had to leave, and the following year a treaty made the exchange of populations official. Around one point two million refugees came to a country of about five million people, most of them women, children and the elderly. Athens took them in wherever it could, in schools, churches and warehouses, and even in the boxes of the old Municipal Theatre, a few streets from here.
Over the following years, they built whole new neighbourhoods on the edges of the city and named them after the places they had lost: Nea Smyrni, New Smyrna, and Nea Ionia, and Nea Filadelfeia. They brought their trades and their spices, dishes like the cumin-scented meatballs called soutzoukakia, and the music that became rebetiko, the Greek blues, sung in small cafés late at night. Within a generation they were simply part of what it means to be Athenian, and a great many families here have a grandmother from Asia Minor, and her recipes.
On the corners, look for the kiosks, the periptera. The first appeared around nineteen eleven, and before long licences to run them were given to men wounded in the wars, in place of a pension. A widow or a child could inherit the licence. Generations of kiosk keepers have sat inside those tiny boxes from early morning till late at night, selling newspapers and cigarettes, sweets and bus tickets, cold water and aspirin, with directions thrown in for free. There are fewer of them now, but they're still the city's corner shop and, for many older Athenians, the place for a daily chat.
In the older cafés around the square, you'll still find men lingering over a tiny cup of Greek coffee, boiled in a small long-handled pot and drunk slowly, leaving the grounds at the bottom of the cup. Some people still turn the cup over and read their fortune in them.

title: Silk and Clay
short: This neighbourhood is called Metaxourgeio, the silk works, after a mill that ran here from the eighteen fifties to the eighteen seventies and employed hundreds of people, most of them women and girls. Its building is now the city's Municipal Gallery. Just to the south lies Kerameikos, the ancient potters' quarter, which gave us the word ceramic. Potters settled there for the clay along a small stream, and its old cemetery holds some of the gentlest family gravestones in Athens.
long:
This square is named for a hero of the War of Independence, Georgios Karaiskakis, but the neighbourhood around it takes its name from something much more domestic: silk. Metaxourgeio means the silk works. In the eighteen fifties a company turned a large building here into a silk mill, and at its busiest it employed more than four hundred workers, most of them women and girls, reeling and twisting the fine thread. For a time it was the largest factory of its kind in Greece. In the eighteen seventies cheaper silk from China arrived and the mill closed, but the name stayed. The building has been restored, and now it's the city's Municipal Gallery.
Just to the south is one of the quietest places in central Athens, the archaeological site of Kerameikos. It was the potters' quarter of the ancient city, and it gave us our word ceramic. The potters came for the clay along the banks of the Eridanos, a little stream that still trickles through the site, and for centuries their workshops and kilns smoked here, turning out cups, jugs and storage jars, and the black and red painted vases that now sit in museums all over the world. The painters often signed their work, and some added little notes praising the good looks of someone they admired.
Just outside the old city gate, along the roads leading out of town, was where Athenians buried their families, and the potters' quarter grew up alongside the cemetery. Many of the gravestones show quiet farewells: two people clasping hands, a mother with her child, a woman with her jewellery box. The stone of Hegeso, which you can see at the National Archaeological Museum, was found here. Today it's a peaceful place of grass and old stones, with wildflowers in spring, frogs in the stream, and the odd tortoise making its way between the graves.
Metaxourgeio today is a mixed and changing neighbourhood. You'll find old neoclassical houses, some crumbling and some beautifully restored, alongside small theatres, galleries, street art and family-run tavernas. Older residents and newcomers live side by side, and artists have been drawn here by lower rents and big old rooms.
So as the bus passes, you're between two old kinds of making, the silk that women spun here a century and a half ago, and the clay that potters shaped just down the road more than two and a half thousand years ago.

title: Cobblers, Gardens and the Evening Stroll
where: A14 Thission (extra stop) and Monastiraki, along Ermou
short: Monastiraki has been a marketplace for a very long time, and its flea market still spills into the lanes. Just beyond is the Ancient Agora, where archaeologists found a workshop floor scattered with shoemaker's nails and a cup marked with the name Simon, a cobbler whose workshop Socrates is said to have visited. And at dusk, the pedestrian street towards Thissio fills with Athenians on their evening stroll, the volta, with the Acropolis glowing above them.
long:
Monastiraki takes its name from the little monastery church that still sits in its square, and the area has been a marketplace for a very long time. In the lanes around Avyssinias Square, the flea market sells everything from copper pots and old records to lace, furniture and army surplus, and on Sundays it spills out into the streets. Near the square stand the walls of Hadrian's Library, built by the emperor in the second century as a quiet place of books and gardens around a long pool.
Beyond the railway line is the Ancient Agora, the heart of the old city, its marketplace and its meeting place, where people came to shop, to settle disputes and to gossip. Near one corner, archaeologists found a small house and workshop whose floor was scattered with iron hobnails, the kind used in the soles of sandals, along with the base of a cup scratched with the name Simon. Ancient writers tell of Simon the shoemaker, at whose workshop Socrates would sit and talk with young men who weren't yet old enough to take part in the business of the Agora. It's a lovely thought, that some of the first philosophy may have been done to the tap of a cobbler's hammer.
On the low hill above the Agora stands the Temple of Hephaestus, the god of metalworkers and craftsmen, one of the best-preserved Greek temples anywhere, with bronze-smiths and potters once working all around it. In the nineteen thirties, an American archaeologist named Dorothy Burr Thompson found rows of pits cut into the rock around the temple, with bits of flowerpots in them. They showed that more than two thousand years ago there had been a garden here. In nineteen fifty-six the garden was replanted, and today shrubs and trees grow around the temple much as they once did. The Agora's cats approve, and doze in its shade.
In the evening, walk along Apostolou Pavlou, the pedestrian street that curves from Thissio along the foot of the hills. This is where Athenians take the volta, the slow evening stroll: grandparents arm in arm, couples, children on scooters, friends stopping for a drink at a café table while the Acropolis turns gold above them and then lights up.
In summer, the open-air Cine Thission, here since nineteen thirty-five, shows films under the stars, with the floodlit Parthenon just behind the screen. Bring a cardigan; even in Athens, the evenings can surprise you.

title: The City's Kitchen
where: A15 Kotzia Sq., on Athinas by City Hall and the Central Market
short: Along Athinas Street is the Central Market, the Varvakeios, which has fed the city since the eighteen eighties. Under its iron roofs are the fish hall and the butchers, and across the street the fruit and vegetable stalls, with spice, olive and cheese shops in the lanes around. Next door, Kotzia Square was once the site of the Municipal Theatre, where refugee families from Asia Minor sheltered in the theatre boxes in nineteen twenty-two. Today it's an open square in front of City Hall.
long:
This is the Central Market, the Varvakeios, and it's been the city's kitchen since it opened in the eighteen eighties. The covered halls hold the meat and fish markets, where stallholders call out their prices over beds of ice. Across Athinas Street, the fruit and vegetable sellers pile up whatever is in season, figs and grapes at the end of summer, oranges and greens in winter. In the lanes around, small shops sell olives, cheese, dried herbs, beans and spices by weight, much as they have for generations. Early in the morning, the restaurant cooks and the grandmothers arrive first, and both know exactly what they want.
In the hard years after twenty ten, when the debt crisis cut wages and pensions and, at its worst, left more than a quarter of working people without a job, the market was one of the places where you could see the city coping. Shoppers bought a little less and chose more carefully. Many families moved back in together, with a grandparent's pension stretched to feed three generations. In neighbourhoods all over Athens, volunteers set up shared kitchens, food banks and free clinics. Greece left its last bailout programme in twenty eighteen, and life is steadier now, but many families still remember those years every time they write a shopping list.
Opposite is Kotzia Square, with City Hall along one side. For half a century, the square's centrepiece was the grand Municipal Theatre, designed by Ernst Ziller and opened in eighteen eighty-eight. In nineteen twenty-two, refugee families from Asia Minor made their homes in its boxes, a household in each little room. The theatre was pulled down around the start of the Second World War.
When an underground car park was planned in the nineteen eighties, archaeologists dug first, and found an ancient road with the ruts of cart wheels still in its surface, family tombs along its edges, and Roman potters' workshops with their kilns. Part of it has been left open to view at the edge of the square, a reminder that people have been coming and going, making and selling, on this spot for two and a half thousand years.
From here, the bus heads back towards Syntagma, and your loop is nearly complete. If all this talk of the market has made you hungry, the next clip is all about food, and where to find it.
